full_judgment: The question involved in that case was rather simple, whether an ejmali property had been partitioned between two brothers, upon the death of one whom his widow claimed to enjoy her husband's share exclusively. The finding of fact as decided by the lower Appellate Court was conclusive and the High Court's interference therewith in second appeal was held to be without jurisdiction. The principle of law as laid down in Durga Chowdhurani's case was followed in a great number of cases all through and Sayed Ishtiaq Ahmed has referred to three of them namely the cases of Abdul Mazid Vs. Khalil Ahmed, 12 DLR SC 132; Nadir Shah Vs. Lal Shah, PLD 1954 Lah, 447 and Deity Patta bhiramaswamy, Vs. S. Hanymayya, AIR 1959 SC 57. In those cases the Supreme Courts strongly deprecated the tendency in some of the High Courts to exercise the prohibited jurisdiction in second appeal purely on question of fact. Facts of those cases need no], be referred to here but on plain reading of those decisions it will tie clear that no question of law was involved in those decisions attracting the High Court's jurisdiction under section 100 C.P.C
